goals: Explain why organisms are classified and name the ranks of the hierarchy
Classify organisms into the five kingdoms using cell type, body organisation and nutrition
Identify the major divisions of plants, including monocots and dicots, with examples

slides.heading: Diversity: sorting the living world
slides.body_md: Part 1: why we classify, the five kingdoms, and the plant divisions.

visual.alt: Flow from kingdom through phylum, class, order, family and genus to species

slides.narration: Millions of kinds of living things share our planet. To study them, scientists sort them into groups, the way a shopkeeper arranges a store. In this part we learn why we classify, how the groups are arranged from big to small, the five kingdoms of life, and the main groups of plants.

slides.heading: Why do we classify?
slides.body_md: Classification means **sorting organisms into groups** by their similarities and differences. It makes the study of millions of species easier, shows how organisms are related, and lets us predict features of a new organism once we know its group.

rows: Shelves of a grocery store: grains, pulses, spices
A shelf for rice, another for wheat
Finding a packet without searching every shelf
Naming and finding an organism quickly

visual.alt: Table comparing sorting in a grocery store with classifying organisms

slides.narration: Think of a grocery store. Grains, pulses and spices each have their own shelf, so you find a packet quickly. Classifying organisms works the same way. It makes the study of millions of kinds of organisms easier, it shows how they are related, and when we meet a new organism we can guess many of its features from its group.

slides.heading: The hierarchy of ranks
slides.body_md: Groups are nested, from the biggest to the smallest: **kingdom, phylum (division in plants), class, order, family, genus, species**. A species is a group of organisms that can breed together and produce fertile offspring. Each step down has fewer organisms and more shared features.

visual.alt: Table of the seven ranks of classification for the tiger and the mango tree

slides.narration: The groups are nested like boxes inside boxes. The largest is the kingdom, then phylum, class, order, family, genus and finally species. Look at the tiger. It is in kingdom Animalia, phylum Chordata and class Mammalia, and it goes on down to its own species. Going down the list, there are fewer organisms in each group, and they share more features.

slides.heading: Worked example: who is the closest relative?
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** The table lists four animals. Which two are the closest relatives, and which is the most distant from the tiger?

**Step 1.** Find the lowest rank that the animals share. The lower the shared rank, the closer the relationship.

**Step 2.** Tiger and lion share the genus *Panthera*, so they are closest. The cat shares only the family Felidae with them.

**Step 3.** The wolf shares only the order Carnivora with the tiger, so it is the most distant.

visual.alt: Table of tiger, lion, domestic cat and wolf with their genus, family and order

slides.narration: Let us find the closest relatives. Look for the lowest rank that animals share. The tiger and the lion share the same genus, Panthera, so they are closest. The domestic cat shares only the family with them. The wolf belongs to a different family and shares only the order with the tiger, so it is the most distant relative of the four.

slides.body_md: Reason with the hierarchy.
slides.narration: Quick check. Remember that animals in the same group share all the ranks above that group.

slides.heading: Five kingdoms of Whittaker
slides.body_md: In 1969 R. H. Whittaker grouped all living things into **five kingdoms**, using three questions: is the **cell prokaryotic or eukaryotic**, is the body **one cell or many cells**, and how does it get **food**?

visual.caption: The five kingdoms: schematic.

slides.narration: In nineteen sixty nine, R H Whittaker placed all living things into five kingdoms. He asked three questions. Is the cell prokaryotic or eukaryotic? Is the body a single cell or made of many cells? And how does the organism get its food? The answers sort life into Monera, Protista, Fungi, Plantae and Animalia.

slides.heading: The three questions side by side
slides.body_md: Only Monera are **prokaryotic**. Plants make food; animals and fungi cannot. Cell walls differ too: **cellulose** in plants, **chitin** in fungi, none in animals.

visual.alt: Table comparing the five kingdoms on nucleus, number of cells, cell wall and food making

slides.narration: This table shows the answers side by side. Only Monera have cells without a nucleus. Monera and Protista are single celled, while plants and animals are many celled. Plants have cellulose cell walls and make their own food. Fungi have walls of chitin and absorb ready made food. Animals have no cell wall and eat other organisms.

slides.heading: Monera and Protista
slides.body_md: Both are mostly **single-celled**. Monera cells have **no nucleus**. Protista cells have a **true nucleus** and organelles. *Euglena* has chloroplasts but also takes in food, so it shows both kinds of nutrition.

rows: Prokaryotic: no nucleus, no organelles with membranes
Some make food (cyanobacteria); others absorb it
Some make food (Euglena); others ingest it (Amoeba)

visual.alt: Table comparing kingdom Monera and kingdom Protista

slides.narration: Monera and Protista are mostly single celled. Monera, such as bacteria and cyanobacteria, have no nucleus. Protista, such as Amoeba, Paramecium and Euglena, have a true nucleus and membrane bound organelles. Some members of both kingdoms make their own food and others take it in. Euglena is interesting, because it has chloroplasts but can also take in food.

slides.heading: Fungi, Plantae and Animalia
slides.body_md: Fungi are not plants: they have **no chlorophyll** and absorb food from dead matter or living hosts. Their cell wall is made of **chitin**.

rows: Many cells; root, stem, leaf in most
Absorb ready-made food from dead or living matter

visual.alt: Table comparing the kingdoms Fungi, Plantae and Animalia

slides.narration: Now the three many celled kingdoms. Fungi, such as mushrooms and bread mould, have walls of chitin, no chlorophyll, and absorb ready made food. Plants have cellulose walls and make food by photosynthesis. Animals have no cell wall and eat other organisms. A mushroom grows from the soil, but it is not a plant, because it cannot make its own food.

slides.heading: Worked example: which kingdom?
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** Place organisms P, Q and R in kingdoms.

**Step 1.** Ask the nucleus question first. Only Q has no nucleus, so Q is in **Monera** (a cyanobacterium).

**Step 2.** P has a nucleus and is a single cell, so it is a **Protista** (like *Euglena*).

**Step 3.** R is many-celled with a chitin wall and absorbs food, so it is in **Fungi**.

rows: Makes own food and also ingests food

visual.alt: Table of three unknown organisms with their nucleus, cell number, cell wall and food

slides.narration: Let us place three organisms. First ask whether there is a nucleus. Organism Q has none, so it is in Monera. Organism P has a nucleus and is a single cell, and it can both make and take in food, so it is a protist like Euglena. Organism R is many celled with a chitin wall and absorbs ready made food, so it belongs to Fungi.

slides.heading: Classifying plants: divisions
slides.body_md: Kingdom Plantae is divided by body structure and by whether seeds are made. **Cryptogams** have no seeds: Thallophyta, Bryophyta, Pteridophyta. **Phanerogams** make seeds: gymnosperms and angiosperms.

visual.caption: The plant divisions: schematic.

slides.narration: Plants are divided by their body structure and by whether they make seeds. The cryptogams do not make seeds, and they are the thallophytes, bryophytes and pteridophytes. The phanerogams make seeds, and they are the gymnosperms and the angiosperms. Angiosperms are divided again into monocots and dicots. The chart reads from simple bodies on the left to the most complex on the right.

slides.heading: Thallophyta and Bryophyta
slides.body_md: Thallophytes are the **algae**, with a body called a **thallus**. Bryophytes are the **amphibians of the plant kingdom**: they live on land but need water to reproduce, and have no vascular tissue.

rows: Thallus: no root, stem or leaf
Stem-like and leaf-like parts; no true roots

visual.alt: Table comparing Thallophyta and Bryophyta

slides.narration: Thallophytes are the algae, such as Spirogyra. Their body, called a thallus, has no root, stem or leaf. Bryophytes, such as moss and liverwort, live on damp land. They are called the amphibians of the plant kingdom, because they need water to reproduce. They have no vascular tissue, so they stay small and close to the ground.

slides.heading: Pteridophyta and gymnosperms
slides.body_md: Both have **vascular tissue** (xylem and phloem) and true roots, stems and leaves. Pteridophytes reproduce by **spores**. Gymnosperms make **naked seeds**, often in cones, and have no fruit.

rows: True root, stem, leaves; often tall trees

visual.alt: Table comparing Pteridophyta and gymnosperms

slides.narration: Pteridophytes, such as ferns, have a true root, stem and leaves with vascular tissue, but they reproduce by spores and make no seeds. Gymnosperms, such as pine and deodar, also have vascular tissue, but they make seeds. Their seeds are naked, which means they are not enclosed in a fruit. They are carried in cones.

slides.heading: Angiosperms: monocots and dicots
slides.body_md: Angiosperms are **flowering plants** whose seeds are **enclosed in fruits**. They are the largest group. A seed has one or two **cotyledons** (seed leaves), which divides angiosperms into monocots and dicots.

visual.alt: Table comparing monocots and dicots

slides.narration: Angiosperms are the flowering plants, and their seeds are enclosed in fruits. They are the largest group of plants. Their seeds have one or two cotyledons, which are the seed leaves. Monocots, such as wheat and maize, have one cotyledon, parallel veins in the leaf, and fibrous roots. Dicots, such as gram and neem, have two cotyledons, net like veins and a tap root.

slides.heading: Quick check: plants
slides.body_md: Place a plant in its division.
slides.narration: Quick check. Ask whether the plant has vascular tissue, whether it makes seeds, and whether the seeds are in a fruit.

slides.heading: Summary: Part 1
bullets: Classification sorts organisms into nested groups: kingdom, phylum, class, order, family, genus, species.
Whittaker used cell type, body organisation and nutrition to make five kingdoms.
Monera are the only prokaryotes. Fungi have chitin walls and absorb food. Plants make food.
Plants: thallophytes, bryophytes, pteridophytes (no seeds); gymnosperms (naked seeds); angiosperms (seeds in fruits).
Angiosperms are monocots (one cotyledon, parallel veins) or dicots (two cotyledons, net veins).

visual.alt: Summary table of one-line tests for five groups

slides.narration: Let us recall. Classification sorts organisms into nested groups from kingdom down to species. Whittaker used cell type, body organisation and nutrition to make five kingdoms. Only Monera are prokaryotes. Plants are divided into thallophytes, bryophytes, pteridophytes, gymnosperms and angiosperms, and angiosperms are monocots or dicots.

bullets: Write the ranks in order, from kingdom to species, and give an example with each rank.
For kingdoms, give the three criteria: cell type, body organisation, nutrition.
Do not say fungi are plants, and do not say that all bacteria are harmful.
For monocot and dicot, give at least three differences: cotyledons, veins, roots.
Give one example for every plant division: Spirogyra, moss, fern, pine, mango.

visual.caption: The animal groups: schematic.

slides.narration: All animals are many celled, have no cell wall, and eat other organisms. They are divided into phyla. Eight phyla have no backbone, from the sponges to the starfish. The phylum Chordata has a notochord, and its main members, the vertebrates, have a backbone and fall into five classes. The classes are fish, amphibians, reptiles, birds and mammals.

slides.heading: Animals without a backbone
slides.body_md: Match each phylum with its key feature and an example. **Arthropoda** is the largest phylum: insects, spiders, prawns and scorpions all have jointed legs.

rows: Pores over the body; no true tissues; fixed
Two cell layers; stinging cells; mouth with tentacles
Soft body, muscular foot, usually a shell

visual.alt: Table of eight invertebrate phyla with a key feature and example for each

slides.narration: Here are the eight phyla without a backbone. Sponges have pores over the body. Hydra and jellyfish have stinging cells. Tapeworms are flat and roundworms are round. Earthworms have bodies in rings. Arthropods have jointed legs, and form the largest phylum. Snails have a soft body and a shell, and starfish have spiny skin.

slides.heading: Chordata and the five vertebrate classes
slides.body_md: Chordates have a **notochord**, a hollow nerve cord on the back, and gill slits at some stage. **Vertebrates** have a backbone. Fish and amphibians depend on water for eggs; reptiles, birds and mammals have adaptations for land.

visual.alt: Table of five vertebrate classes with skin, breathing, heart chambers and examples

slides.narration: Chordates have a notochord, a nerve cord along the back, and gill slits at some stage of life. In vertebrates the notochord is replaced by a backbone. Fish breathe with gills and have scales. Frogs have moist skin and start life in water. Reptiles have dry scales, birds have feathers, and mammals have hair and feed their young with milk.

slides.heading: Worked example: which group?
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** Name the group of each animal in the table.

**X.** Body in rings and lives in soil: phylum **Annelida** (an earthworm).

**Y.** Backbone, feathers and hard-shelled eggs: class **Aves** (a bird).

**Z.** Backbone, gills and fins and a two-chambered heart: class **Pisces** (a fish).

Start with the backbone question: if there is none, it is an invertebrate phylum.

visual.alt: Table of three unknown animals with three clues each

slides.narration: Let us name three groups. Animal X has a body in rings and lives in soil, so it is an annelid, like an earthworm. Animal Y has a backbone, feathers and lays hard shelled eggs, so it is a bird. Animal Z has a backbone, gills, fins and a two chambered heart, so it is a fish. Always ask first whether there is a backbone.

slides.heading: Quick check: animal groups
slides.body_md: Place an animal in a phylum.
slides.narration: Quick check. Look for the single clue that fits one group only, such as jointed legs or a muscular foot.

slides.heading: Binomial nomenclature
slides.body_md: Carolus **Linnaeus** gave every organism a two-part name: **genus** then **species**. The name is in Latin form and is the same all over the world, so a tamarind is *Tamarindus indica* whether you call it imli, chinch or puli.

visual.alt: Table of five common names with their scientific names and genus

slides.narration: Common names change from place to place. The tamarind is imli in Hindi, chinch in Marathi and puli in Tamil. So Carolus Linnaeus gave every organism a two part scientific name, made of the genus and the species, in Latin form. This system is called binomial nomenclature. The name is the same all over the world, which avoids confusion.

slides.heading: Rules for writing a scientific name
slides.body_md: The **genus** starts with a **capital letter**; the **species** starts with a **small letter**. In print the whole name is in *italics*; when handwritten, **underline each word separately**.

rows: Genus begins with a capital letter
Species begins with a small letter
Italics in print; underline each word when handwritten
Mangifera indica in italics, or Mangifera indica with each word underlined

visual.alt: Table of rules for writing scientific names, with a wrong and a right example for each

slides.narration: Follow these rules. A scientific name has two words, the genus first and the species second. The genus starts with a capital letter, and the species starts with a small letter. In print, the name is set in italics. When you write it by hand, underline the genus and the species separately. In plain text, like narration, we simply say the two words.

slides.heading: Worked example: correct the names
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** Correct each written name.

**1.** *panthera Leo*: the genus needs a capital and the species a small letter, so *Panthera leo* (lion).

**2.** *Homo Sapiens*: the species must be small, so *Homo sapiens* (human).

**3.** *Azadirachta*: only the genus is given, so add the species: *Azadirachta indica* (neem).

rows: Genus needs a capital; species needs a small letter
Species name must start with a small letter
Only the genus is given; a species name is missing

visual.alt: Table of three wrongly written scientific names, the problem in each and the corrected name

slides.narration: Let us correct three names. The first has the capital letters in the wrong places, so it becomes Panthera leo, the lion. In the second, the species word should start with a small letter, so it becomes Homo sapiens. The third gives only the genus, so we add the species word to get Azadirachta indica, the neem tree. A full name always needs both words.

slides.body_md: Choose the correct way to write a name.
slides.narration: Quick check. Recall which word begins with a capital letter and which with a small letter.

slides.narration: A virus is a tiny particle. It has genetic material, either DNA or RNA, packed inside a protein coat called the capsid. A virus has no cytoplasm, no organelles and no cell membrane, so we say it is acellular. It is also very small. A typical virus is about twenty times smaller than a bacterium.

slides.heading: Why viruses have no kingdom
slides.body_md: Whittaker's kingdoms group **cells**. A virus is **not a cell**, cannot make its own proteins and **multiplies only inside a host cell**. Outside, it is inactive. So it does not fit any of the five kingdoms.

rows: Cell with cytoplasm and a membrane

visual.alt: Table comparing a bacterium and a virus

slides.narration: The five kingdoms sort cells. A virus is not a cell. It cannot make its own proteins, and it cannot multiply on its own. It can multiply only by entering a living host cell and using the cell to make copies of itself. Outside a host it is inactive. Since it does not behave as a complete living cell, it has no place in any of the five kingdoms.

slides.heading: How a virus multiplies
slides.body_md: A virus **attaches** to a host cell, its genetic material **enters**, the host is **forced to copy** it, and new viruses **burst out**. This harms the host cell and can cause disease.

slides.narration: This is how a virus multiplies. It attaches to a host cell. Its genetic material enters the cell. The cell is then forced to make copies of the virus. Finally the new viruses burst out and can infect other cells. This is why viruses are called particles that live only by taking over a host.

slides.body_md: **Producers** make food by photosynthesis and start every food chain. **Consumers** eat other organisms. **Decomposers** break down dead remains and wastes and return nutrients to the soil.

slides.narration: In any habitat, organisms play three roles. Producers, such as grass and trees, make food using sunlight. Consumers, such as the grasshopper, goat, frog and eagle, eat other organisms. Decomposers, mainly bacteria and fungi, break down dead plants, dead animals and wastes. slides.heading: Fungi and bacteria at work
slides.body_md: Fungi and bacteria are **nature's recyclers**: without them, dead leaves and bodies would pile up and nutrients would stay locked. Many are also useful to people, while some cause disease or spoil food.

Cause diseases such as typhoid and cholera
Decompose litter; yeast makes dough rise
Moulds spoil bread; some cause skin infections

visual.alt: Table of useful and harmful roles of bacteria and fungi

slides.narration: Fungi and bacteria are nature recyclers. They decompose dead leaves and bodies, so nutrients return to the soil for plants to use. Many are useful to us. Bacteria turn milk into curd and help pulse plants, and yeast, a fungus, makes dough rise. But some bacteria cause diseases, and moulds spoil bread. So the same kingdoms can help us or harm us.

slides.heading: Worked example: roles in a pond
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** Give the role of each organism in the pond table, and say how many times longer a 2000 nm bacterium is than a 100 nm virus.

**Roles.** Algae make food: **producer**. A tadpole eats algae: **herbivore** consumer. A fish eats the tadpole: **carnivore** consumer. Bacteria in the mud break down dead remains: **decomposer**.

**Size.** $\dfrac{2000\ \text{nm}}{100\ \text{nm}} = 20$ times.

slides.narration: Let us assign roles in a pond. The tiny algae make food, so they are producers. The tadpole eats the algae, so it is a herbivore consumer. The fish eats the tadpole, so it is a carnivore consumer. Bacteria in the mud break down dead remains, so they are decomposers. Also, a bacterium of two thousand nanometres is twenty times longer than a virus of one hundred nanometres.

sections.heading: 1. Why we classify, and the hierarchy
sections.body_md:
**Classification** is the sorting of organisms into groups by their similarities and differences. It makes the study of millions of species easier, shows how organisms are related, and lets us predict the features of a new organism from its group.

The groups are nested: **kingdom, phylum (division in plants), class, order, family, genus, species**. Each step down has fewer organisms that share more features. A **species** is a group of organisms that can breed with each other and produce fertile offspring. Animals that share a lower rank are closer relatives: the tiger (*Panthera tigris*) and the lion (*Panthera leo*) share a genus, but the domestic cat (*Felis catus*) shares only the family.

key_terms.definition_md: Sorting organisms into groups by their similarities and differences.

sections.heading: 2. Five-kingdom classification
sections.body_md:
In 1969 R. H. Whittaker placed all organisms in **five kingdoms**, using three criteria: **cell type** (prokaryotic or eukaryotic), **body organisation** (one cell or many cells) and **mode of nutrition** (makes food or takes it in).

- **Monera:** prokaryotic, single-celled; bacteria and cyanobacteria.
- **Protista:** eukaryotic, single-celled; *Amoeba*, *Paramecium*, *Euglena*.
- **Fungi:** eukaryotic, mostly many-celled threads, chitin wall, absorb ready-made food; mushroom, bread mould, yeast (one-celled).
- **Plantae:** eukaryotic, many-celled, cellulose wall, photosynthesis.
- **Animalia:** eukaryotic, many-celled, no cell wall, eat other organisms.

The tough material that forms the cell wall of fungi.
An organism that makes its own food, such as a green plant.

sections.heading: 3. Major divisions of plants
sections.body_md:
Plants are divided by body structure and by whether they make seeds.

**Cryptogams (no seeds):** **Thallophyta** (algae such as *Spirogyra*; body is a thallus with no root, stem or leaf); **Bryophyta** (moss, liverwort; need water to reproduce; no vascular tissue); **Pteridophyta** (ferns; vascular tissue, spores, no seeds).

**Phanerogams (make seeds):** **Gymnosperms** (pine, deodar, *Cycas*; naked seeds in cones) and **Angiosperms** (flowering plants; seeds inside fruits). Angiosperms are **monocots** (one cotyledon, parallel veins, fibrous roots: wheat, maize) or **dicots** (two cotyledons, net-like veins, tap root: gram, neem).

key_terms.definition_md: A plant body that is not divided into root, stem and leaf.
Xylem and phloem, which carry water and food through a plant.
A seed leaf inside a seed.
A flowering plant whose seeds are enclosed in a fruit.

sections.heading: 4. Major groups of animals
sections.body_md:
**Invertebrates (no backbone):** **Porifera** (sponges; pores), **Cnidaria** (*Hydra*, jellyfish; stinging cells), **Platyhelminthes** (flatworms), **Nematoda** (roundworms), **Annelida** (earthworm; rings), **Arthropoda** (jointed legs; the largest phylum), **Mollusca** (snail; soft body, foot, shell) and **Echinodermata** (starfish; spiny skin).

**Chordata** have a notochord, a nerve cord on the back and gill slits at some stage. **Vertebrates** have a backbone and fall into five classes: **Pisces** (scales, gills), **Amphibia** (moist skin, water and land), **Reptilia** (dry scales), **Aves** (feathers, four-chambered heart) and **Mammalia** (hair, milk glands, mostly give birth to young).

sections.heading: 5. Binomial nomenclature
sections.body_md:
Carolus **Linnaeus** introduced the **two-part scientific name**: the **genus** and then the **species**, in Latin form. It is the same all over the world, so it removes the confusion caused by local names (imli, chinch, puli: all *Tamarindus indica*).

**Rules:**
1. The name has two words, genus first.
2. The genus begins with a **capital letter**; the species begins with a **small letter**.
3. In print the name is in *italics*. When handwritten, **underline the genus and the species separately**.

Examples: *Homo sapiens* (human), *Panthera tigris* (tiger), *Mangifera indica* (mango), *Azadirachta indica* (neem). The same species word (*indica*) can appear in different genera; the **full two-word name** is unique.

sections.heading: 6. Viruses: acellular entities
sections.body_md:
A **virus** is genetic material (DNA or RNA) inside a **protein coat** (capsid), sometimes with spikes. It has **no cytoplasm, no organelles and no cell membrane**, so it is **acellular**. A virus cannot make its own proteins and **multiplies only inside a host cell**; outside a host it is inactive. Typical viruses are about 20 to 300 nm, much smaller than bacteria (about 2000 nm).

**Why no kingdom?** Whittaker's kingdoms group cells. Viruses are not cells and do not carry out life processes on their own, so they are not placed in any of the five kingdoms.

key_terms.definition_md: An acellular particle of genetic material in a protein coat that multiplies only inside a host cell.
Not made of cells.

sections.heading: 7. Ecological roles of organisms
sections.body_md:
**Producers** (green plants, algae, cyanobacteria) make food by photosynthesis. **Consumers** (herbivores, carnivores, omnivores) eat other organisms. **Decomposers**, mainly **bacteria and fungi**, break down dead remains and wastes and return nutrients to the soil.

**Fungi and bacteria** are useful (decomposition, curd, bread, helping pulse crops) and harmful (diseases, spoiled food). Arrows in a food chain point from the **food to the eater**.

key_terms.definition_md: An organism that makes its own food, usually by photosynthesis.
An organism that eats other organisms.
A bacterium or fungus that breaks down dead remains and wastes.

rows: Break down dead remains and wastes and absorb the products

notes.exam_tips_md:
**Common mistakes**
- Calling fungi plants, or writing that fungi make food by photosynthesis.
- Writing the species word with a capital letter, or forgetting to italicise or underline.
- Saying that bryophytes have xylem and phloem.
- Writing that gymnosperms bear fruits, or that a bat is a bird.
- Calling a virus a cell, or placing a virus in Monera.
- Drawing food chain arrows from the eater to the food.

**How marks are usually awarded**
- 1-mark items: a name, a place in a group, or one feature.
- 2-mark items: two points, one mark each.
- 3-mark items: three short correct points with an example.
- 5-mark items: a labelled chart or table and clear points with examples.

cards.front_md: Give two reasons why we classify organisms.
cards.back_md: It makes the study of millions of species easier, and it shows how organisms are related.

cards.front_md: List the ranks of classification from largest to smallest.
cards.back_md: Kingdom, phylum (division), class, order, family, genus, species.

cards.front_md: What is a species?
cards.back_md: A group of organisms that can breed together and produce fertile offspring.

cards.front_md: Who proposed the five-kingdom classification, and when?
cards.back_md: R. H. Whittaker, in 1969.

cards.front_md: What three criteria did Whittaker use?
cards.back_md: Cell type, body organisation and mode of nutrition.

cards.front_md: Which is the only prokaryotic kingdom?
cards.back_md: Monera.

cards.front_md: Name two examples of Protista.
cards.back_md: Amoeba, Paramecium, Euglena (any two).

cards.front_md: What is the cell wall of fungi made of?
cards.back_md: Chitin.

cards.front_md: Why are fungi not plants?
cards.back_md: They have no chlorophyll and absorb ready-made food instead of making it.

cards.front_md: Which kingdom has many-celled organisms with no cell wall that eat other organisms?
cards.back_md: Animalia.

cards.front_md: What are cryptogams? Name their three divisions.
cards.back_md: Plants without seeds: Thallophyta, Bryophyta, Pteridophyta.

cards.front_md: What is a thallus?
cards.back_md: A plant body that is not divided into root, stem and leaf, as in algae.

cards.front_md: Why are bryophytes called the amphibians of the plant kingdom?
cards.back_md: They live on land but need water to reproduce.

cards.front_md: What do pteridophytes have that bryophytes lack?
cards.back_md: Vascular tissue (xylem and phloem) and true roots, stems and leaves.

cards.front_md: What are naked seeds? Name two gymnosperms.
cards.back_md: Seeds not enclosed in a fruit; pine and deodar (or Cycas).

cards.front_md: What is the main feature of angiosperms?
cards.back_md: Flowers, and seeds enclosed in fruits.

cards.front_md: Give three differences between monocots and dicots.
cards.back_md: One or two cotyledons; parallel or net-like veins; fibrous or tap roots.

cards.front_md: Which animal phylum is the largest, and what is its key feature?
cards.back_md: Arthropoda; jointed legs and a hard outer covering.

cards.front_md: Name the phylum of sponges and one feature.
cards.back_md: Porifera; pores over the body.

cards.front_md: Which phylum has stinging cells? Give an example.
cards.back_md: Cnidaria; Hydra or jellyfish.

cards.front_md: What do mollusca have in common?
cards.back_md: A soft body, a muscular foot, and usually a shell (snail, octopus).

cards.front_md: What features define Chordata?
cards.back_md: A notochord, a nerve cord on the back and gill slits at some stage.

cards.front_md: Name the five classes of vertebrates.
cards.back_md: Pisces, Amphibia, Reptilia, Aves, Mammalia.

cards.front_md: Three features of mammals?
cards.back_md: Hair, milk glands and a four-chambered heart.

cards.front_md: Who introduced binomial nomenclature?
cards.back_md: Carolus Linnaeus.

cards.front_md: State the rules for writing a scientific name.
cards.back_md: Genus first with a capital letter, species second with a small letter; italics in print, underline each word by hand.

cards.front_md: Write the scientific names of human, tiger and mango.
cards.back_md: Homo sapiens, Panthera tigris, Mangifera indica.

cards.front_md: Why are viruses called acellular?
cards.back_md: They have no cytoplasm, organelles or cell membrane: only genetic material in a protein coat.

cards.front_md: Why are viruses not placed in any kingdom?
cards.back_md: They are not cells and multiply only inside a host cell.

cards.front_md: Name the three ecological roles and one example of each.
cards.back_md: Producer (grass), consumer (goat), decomposer (fungus or bacterium).

cards.front_md: Give one useful and one harmful role of bacteria.
cards.back_md: Useful: curd or decomposition. Harmful: diseases such as typhoid.

questions.stem_md: Two animals belong to the same family but to different genera. Which statement must be true for them?

options.text_md: They share the same kingdom, phylum, class and order.
They belong to the same species.
They belong to the same genus.

questions.solution_md: Ranks nest inside one another. Animals in the same family must also be in the same order, class, phylum and kingdom — option (a). Different genera means they are not in the same genus or species.

questions.stem_md: A student suggests sorting all living things first by habitat: those that live in water and those that live on land. Why would scientists reject this as a first step?

options.text_md: Organisms with very different fundamental features, such as a whale and a shark, would be placed together.
Water and land cannot be told apart in nature.
Every organism in water belongs to the same kingdom.
Habitat never has any effect on an organism.

questions.solution_md: Classification starts with fundamental features such as cell type, body organisation and nutrition. Habitat would group a whale with a shark although they differ in many basic features — option (a).

questions.stem_md: A one-celled organism from pond water has a clear nucleus and no cell wall, and it moves by pushing out false feet and engulfing bacteria. Which kingdom does it belong to?
questions.solution_md: A nucleus rules out Monera. One cell and no cell wall rule out Fungi and Plantae. A one-celled eukaryote like this Amoeba is a protist — option (d).

questions.stem_md: A forester finds a shelf-shaped growth on a rotting tree stump. Its cells have walls of chitin, it has no chlorophyll, and it absorbs food from the dead wood. It belongs to kingdom:
questions.solution_md: A chitin cell wall, no chlorophyll and absorption of ready-made food are the features of Fungi — option (a). Plants have cellulose walls and make food; animals have no wall.

questions.stem_md: Cyanobacteria make food by photosynthesis, like green plants, yet they are placed in Monera and not in Plantae. The best reason is that:

options.text_md: their cells have no nucleus and no membrane-bound organelles
they are too small to be seen with the eye

questions.solution_md: Cell type is the first criterion. Cyanobacteria are prokaryotes, so they go in Monera even though they photosynthesise — option (a). Many bacteria do have a cell wall, and living in water does not decide the kingdom.

questions.stem_md: Baker’s yeast is one-celled and has a nucleus, yet it is placed in kingdom Fungi and not Protista. Which feature is the best reason?

options.text_md: It is made of a single cell.
It has a cell wall of chitin and absorbs ready-made food.
It is used to make dough rise.

questions.solution_md: Protists also have one cell and a nucleus, so those cannot decide the kingdom. A chitin wall and absorption of food are features of Fungi — option (b).

questions.stem_md: Which row correctly matches each kingdom with its usual mode of nutrition?

options.text_md: Plantae: eating other organisms; Fungi: photosynthesis; Animalia: absorbing ready-made food
Plantae: absorbing ready-made food; Fungi: eating other organisms; Animalia: photosynthesis
Plantae: photosynthesis; Fungi: absorbing ready-made food; Animalia: eating other organisms
Plantae: photosynthesis; Fungi: photosynthesis; Animalia: absorbing ready-made food

questions.solution_md: Plants make food by photosynthesis, fungi absorb ready-made food, and animals eat other organisms — option (c).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Bacteria are placed in kingdom Monera.

**Reason (R):** Bacterial cells have no true nucleus and no membrane-bound organelles.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: Monera is the kingdom of prokaryotes, and bacteria are prokaryotes because they have no true nucleus and no membrane-bound organelles. R explains A — option (a).

questions.stem_md: True or false? The cell wall of a mushroom is made of chitin and not of cellulose.
questions.solution_md: True. Fungal cell walls contain chitin, while plant cell walls are made of cellulose.

questions.stem_md: True or false? In the scientific name *Mangifera indica*, only the first word begins with a capital letter.
questions.solution_md: True. The genus name begins with a capital letter and the species name begins with a small letter.

questions.stem_md: A group of organisms that can breed with each other and produce fertile offspring is called a ______.
questions.solution_md: The ability to breed and produce fertile offspring defines a species.

questions.stem_md: Match each kingdom (column I) with an organism in column II.

match_right.text_md: Hydra clinging to a pond weed
A cyanobacterium in a rice field

questions.solution_md: A cyanobacterium is prokaryotic (Monera); Paramecium is a one-celled eukaryote (Protista); chapati mould is a fungus; Hydra is an animal.

questions.stem_md: A student surveys a hill park and records 60 different organisms (given): 27 flowering plants, 9 ferns and mosses together, 15 insects, 6 birds and 3 kinds of mushroom. What percentage of the recorded organisms belong to kingdom Animalia?
questions.solution_md: Animals are the insects and the birds: $15 + 6 = 21$. The mushrooms are fungi and the other organisms are plants. Percentage $= \dfrac{21}{60} \times 100 = 35\%$.

marking_scheme.step: Identifies the animals: 15 insects and 6 birds make 21
Divides by 60 and multiplies by 100 to get 35 %

questions.stem_md: A librarian arranges 5000 books by subject on separate shelves. Give two reasons why biologists, too, arrange organisms into groups.

answer.model_answer_md: Grouping makes it easier to study the millions of kinds of organisms, just as subject shelves make books easy to find. It also shows which organisms are related, so we can guess the features of a new organism from its group.

questions.solution_md: Easier study; shows relationships.

marking_scheme.step: Makes the study of many organisms easier

questions.stem_md: State two differences between the organisms of kingdom Monera and those of kingdom Protista.

answer.model_answer_md: Monera cells are prokaryotic, with no true nucleus and no membrane-bound organelles, whereas Protista cells are eukaryotic with a true nucleus and organelles. Monera include bacteria and cyanobacteria, whereas Protista include Amoeba and Paramecium.

questions.solution_md: Prokaryotic against eukaryotic; examples.

marking_scheme.step: Monera: no true nucleus or membrane-bound organelles; Protista: true nucleus and organelles

questions.stem_md: A mushroom springs up from the soil after the first monsoon rain. Why is it placed in Fungi and not in Plantae?

answer.model_answer_md: A mushroom has no chlorophyll, so it cannot make its own food by photosynthesis. It absorbs ready-made food from dead matter, and its cell wall is made of chitin, not cellulose, so it belongs to Fungi.

questions.solution_md: No chlorophyll and absorbs food; chitin wall.

marking_scheme.step: No chlorophyll, so it absorbs ready-made food
Cell wall of chitin, not cellulose

questions.stem_md: Write the ranks of classification in order from the largest to the smallest. What happens to the number of organisms and to the features they share as we go from kingdom down to species?

answer.model_answer_md: The ranks are kingdom, phylum (or division in plants), class, order, family, genus and species. As we go down, each group contains fewer organisms. The organisms in a lower group share more features, so the species is the most specific group and the kingdom the broadest.

questions.solution_md: Seven ranks in order; fewer organisms; more shared features.

marking_scheme.step: All seven ranks in the right order
Fewer organisms in each lower group
More shared features in each lower group

questions.stem_md: Name the five kingdoms of Whittaker and the three criteria used to form them. For each kingdom, give one feature and one example.

answer.model_answer_md: Whittaker used three criteria: cell type, body organisation and mode of nutrition. Monera are prokaryotic single cells with no nucleus, such as bacteria. Protista are single-celled eukaryotes, such as Amoeba. Fungi are mostly many-celled, have chitin walls and absorb ready-made food, such as mushrooms. Plantae are many-celled eukaryotes with cellulose walls that make food by photosynthesis, such as mango. Animalia are many-celled eukaryotes with no cell wall that eat other organisms, such as a fish.

questions.solution_md: Three criteria; five kingdoms with a feature and an example each.

marking_scheme.step: A correct feature for each kingdom
A correct example for each kingdom

questions.stem_md: A gardener finds a plant in a shady corner. It has a true root, a stem and feathery leaves, and brown spore cases on the underside of the leaves. It has no flowers or seeds. It belongs to:
questions.solution_md: A plant with true roots, stem and leaves and vascular tissue, but with spores instead of seeds, is a pteridophyte — option (a). Bryophytes have no true roots, and the other two groups make seeds.

questions.stem_md: A green carpet of moss grows on a damp wall and never grows tall. Which pair of features explains this?

options.text_md: It has xylem but no phloem, and makes naked seeds.
It has true roots and makes spores in cones.
It has no vascular tissue and needs water for reproduction.
It makes flowers but has no leaves.

questions.solution_md: Bryophytes such as moss have no vascular tissue to carry water upwards and need water to reproduce, so they stay small and near damp places — option (c).

questions.stem_md: Cones of a deodar tree release winged seeds that were never enclosed inside a fruit. This tells us that deodar is a:
questions.solution_md: Plants whose seeds are naked and borne in cones are gymnosperms — option (b). Angiosperm seeds are inside fruits and pteridophytes make no seeds.

questions.stem_md: A seed is split open and has only one seed leaf. The seedling has leaves with parallel veins and a bunch of thin roots of nearly equal size. The plant is most likely:
questions.solution_md: One cotyledon, parallel veins and fibrous roots are features of a monocot such as wheat — option (c). Gram, neem and mustard are dicots.

questions.stem_md: Spirogyra forms green slimy threads in ponds. It is placed in Thallophyta because:

options.text_md: it lives only on dry land
its body is not divided into root, stem and leaf

questions.solution_md: Thallophytes have a simple body, a thallus, with no root, stem or leaf — option (d). They have no vascular tissue and make no seeds.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** A fern can grow taller and carry water to its fronds better than a moss.

**Reason (R):** A fern has vascular tissue, whereas a moss has none.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: Xylem and phloem carry water and food over long distances, so ferns can grow taller than mosses. R explains A — option (a).

questions.stem_md: Plants whose seeds are not enclosed in a fruit are called ______.
questions.solution_md: Gymnosperms have naked seeds, often in cones. Angiosperm seeds are inside fruits.

questions.stem_md: Give two differences between a moss and a fern.

answer.model_answer_md: A fern has true roots, stem and leaves, whereas a moss has no true roots. A fern has vascular tissue to carry water and food, whereas a moss has none and so stays small and close to the damp ground.

questions.solution_md: True roots and vascular tissue in a fern, absent in moss.

marking_scheme.step: True roots, stem and leaves in fern; no true roots in moss
Vascular tissue in fern; none in moss

questions.stem_md: A maize seedling and a gram seedling are placed side by side. Give two features that distinguish them, and name the group of each.

answer.model_answer_md: The maize seedling has one cotyledon and leaves with parallel veins, so it is a monocot. The gram seedling has two cotyledons and leaves with net-like veins, so it is a dicot. Roots are fibrous in maize and a tap root in gram.

questions.solution_md: Cotyledons and veins; monocot and dicot.

marking_scheme.step: Two correct features such as cotyledons and veins

questions.stem_md: A plant has true roots, stem and leaves, xylem and phloem, and makes seeds that are not enclosed in a fruit. Name its division, and explain how it differs from a pteridophyte and from an angiosperm.

answer.model_answer_md: The plant is a gymnosperm. A pteridophyte also has vascular tissue but makes spores and no seeds at all. An angiosperm also makes seeds, but its seeds are enclosed inside a fruit, whereas the seeds of a gymnosperm are naked and carried in cones.

questions.solution_md: Gymnosperm; seeds against spores; naked against enclosed.

marking_scheme.step: Differs from pteridophyte: seeds, not spores
Differs from angiosperm: naked seeds, no fruit

questions.stem_md: Classify the plant kingdom into its major divisions. For each division, give one distinguishing feature and one example.

answer.model_answer_md: The plant kingdom is divided into five divisions. Thallophyta are algae with a body that has no root, stem or leaf, such as Spirogyra. Bryophyta have no vascular tissue and need water to reproduce, such as moss. Pteridophyta have vascular tissue but reproduce by spores and make no seeds, such as fern. Gymnosperms make naked seeds in cones, such as pine. Angiosperms are flowering plants with seeds inside fruits, such as mango, and are divided into monocots, such as wheat, and dicots, such as gram.

questions.solution_md: Five divisions with a feature and an example each.

marking_scheme.step: A correct feature for each division
A correct example for each division
Angiosperms divided into monocots and dicots

questions.stem_md: A slow animal found on a wet garden wall has a soft unsegmented body, a muscular foot and a hard coiled shell. Its phylum is:
questions.solution_md: A soft body, a muscular foot and a shell describe a snail, a mollusc — option (a). Annelids have bodies in rings, arthropods have jointed legs and echinoderms have spiny skin.

questions.stem_md: A butterfly, a scorpion and a prawn look very different, but they are placed in one phylum. They all have:

options.text_md: jointed legs and a hard outer covering
a soft body with a muscular foot

questions.solution_md: Jointed legs and a hard outer covering define phylum Arthropoda — option (b). The other options describe vertebrates, molluscs and cnidarians.

questions.stem_md: An ostrich cannot fly, yet it is placed in class Aves. The best reason is that it:

options.text_md: can run very fast on land
has two legs and a long neck
lives on grasslands in warm regions
has feathers, has forelimbs modified as wings and lays hard-shelled eggs

questions.solution_md: Class Aves is defined by features such as feathers, wings and hard-shelled eggs, not by the ability to fly — option (d).

questions.stem_md: A tadpole breathes with gills in a pond, while the adult frog breathes with lungs and a moist skin and can live on land. A frog is placed in class:
questions.solution_md: Animals that spend part of life in water and part on land, with a moist skin and a change in body form, are amphibians — option (d).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Sponges are plants because they stay fixed in one place.

**Reason (R):** Sponges have pores all over the body and no true tissues.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: Sponges are animals, in phylum Porifera, because they cannot make their own food; being fixed does not make an organism a plant. So A is false. R is a true description of sponges — option (d).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** A bat is placed in class Mammalia, not in class Aves.

**Reason (R):** A bat has wings and can fly, like a bird.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: A bat has hair and milk glands, so it is a mammal, and A is true. R is also true, but flying is not the basis for placing it in Mammalia, so R does not explain A — option (b).

questions.stem_md: True or false? A whale is placed with the fishes because it lives in the sea and has flippers.
questions.solution_md: False. A whale has hair, milk glands and a four-chambered heart and breathes with lungs, so it is a mammal.

questions.stem_md: Animals that have a notochord at some stage of life belong to the phylum ______.
questions.solution_md: Chordata have a notochord, a nerve cord on the back and gill slits at some stage.

questions.stem_md: Match each phylum (column I) with its key feature (column II).

match_right.text_md: Soft body with a muscular foot

questions.solution_md: Porifera have pores; Annelida have ring-like segments; Echinodermata have spiny skin; Mollusca have a soft body and a muscular foot.

questions.stem_md: Name the class to which each belongs: (i) a rohu that breathes with gills and has scales, (ii) a crow that has feathers. State one more feature of each class.

answer.model_answer_md: The rohu is a fish, class Pisces, and it has fins and a two-chambered heart. The crow is a bird, class Aves, and it has a four-chambered heart and lays hard-shelled eggs.

questions.solution_md: Pisces and Aves with a further feature each.

marking_scheme.step: Rohu: Pisces, with one more feature
Crow: Aves, with one more feature

questions.stem_md: Give three differences between a mammal and a reptile, with one example of each.

answer.model_answer_md: A mammal has hair on its skin, whereas a reptile has dry scales. A mammal has mammary glands to feed its young, but a reptile has none. Most mammals give birth to young, whereas reptiles lay eggs. A cow is a mammal and a lizard is a reptile.

questions.solution_md: Hair against scales; milk glands; birth against eggs.

marking_scheme.step: Milk glands against none; birth against eggs

questions.stem_md: Name the phylum of each animal and state one feature that helped you: a sponge, a tapeworm and a starfish.

answer.model_answer_md: The sponge is in phylum Porifera, because its body has many pores and it stays fixed in one place. The tapeworm is in Platyhelminthes, because its body is flat and has no body cavity. The starfish is in Echinodermata, because it has spiny skin and its body is arranged around a centre.

questions.solution_md: Porifera, Platyhelminthes, Echinodermata with a feature each.

questions.stem_md: Name the five classes of vertebrates. For each class, state one distinguishing feature and give one example.

answer.model_answer_md: The five classes of vertebrates are Pisces, Amphibia, Reptilia, Aves and Mammalia. Pisces are fish that live in water, have scales and breathe with gills, such as rohu. Amphibia have moist skin and live on land and in water, such as frog. Reptilia have dry scales and lay eggs on land, such as lizard. Aves have feathers, wings and a four-chambered heart, such as crow. Mammalia have hair and mammary glands, and most give birth to young, such as cow.

questions.solution_md: Five classes with a feature and an example each.

marking_scheme.step: A distinguishing feature for each class
A correct example for each class

questions.stem_md: Read the passage and answer the questions that follow.
questions.passage_md:
A class collects six organisms from a pond and its banks and builds this key. At each step, follow the statement that fits and go where it says. The six organisms are a bacterium, *Paramecium*, *Spirogyra*, a water fern (*Marsilea*), a bread mould and *Hydra*, but the labels P to U do not follow this order.

1a. Body is a single cell: go to 2.
1b. Body has many cells: go to 3.
2a. Cell has no nucleus: **P**.
2b. Cell has a nucleus: **Q**.
3a. Body makes its own food using chlorophyll: go to 4.
3b. Body cannot make its own food: go to 5.
4a. Body is a thread with no root, stem or leaf: **R**.
